THE BUDGET:
Consideration of the motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, resumed from Wednesday, April 22,

Mr. Speaker,'if the Budget, to which it was our privilege to listen some few days ago, had been confined to an exposition of the financial affairs of the country, it would have been my pleasure to have joined in the many encomiums pronounced upon that part of the hon. gentleman's deliverance and to have declared, and declared with perfect sincerity, that it was worthy of all commendation. Barring a
few thrusts which my hon. friend attempted at his opponents, and which his opponents at the present time can very well pass by, the expose of the book-keeping and the business of the Dominion which he presented, the liabilities, the assets and the resulting obligations, was clear, concise and to the point, and if my hon. friend permitted me,
I would offer him my heartiest congratulations.
But as to the othec part in which my hon. friend discussed the economic situation of the country, I must say that-and I shall appeal to the judgment of those who sit behind him-my hon. friend was, as to his facts and conclusions, singularly in error, and failed altogether to rise to a true conception of his duties and of his responsibilities.
My hon. friend stated, as he has done on more than one occasion in the House and out of it, that the economic situation of the country was satisfactory; that we had passed through a period of depression, but of slight depression only as compared with 1907, and that already we were sailing into calmer waters. He stated emphatically that there was no occasion for alarm; that we could well afford to wait in peace for the reaction, and that as regards the amount of reform he would make, it would be simply to tighten the screws upon a few items of the tariff and to make some semblance of reduction upon farm implements, a reduction so insignificant that it in fact adds insult to injury.
My hon. friend, with great complacency, relies upon the enormous resources of Canada. They are enormous indeed, especially in agricultural possibilities; tout my hon. friend, at all events, ought to know-and he is in a position to know more than anyone else in this House-that though the resources of Canada are enormous, and though we have yet hardly touched the fringe of them, at this moment in the eastern provinces agricultural production is not keeping pace with the requirements of the country. As to the western provinces, he knows also that agricultural development is rapidly coming to a standstill. He cannot ignore these facts; but still he turns his back upon the situation. We could not expect anything else, for he is one of those who three years ago so clamorously shouted: ' No change; no improvement; let well enough alone.' The man who-has not the energy to improve never will have the courage to reform

My hon. friend stated, however, that agriculture was the basic industry of all industries. If it is true, as I shall be able to prove later on, that at this moment agriculture is not returning what we have a right to expect from it, is not that proof that there is something ajar in the situation of the country which requires the attention of the Government; and if the Government fail to apply themselves to the task of remedying the situation, then it is also proof that they are not worthy of the confidence that the people have reposed in them?
I am well aware that nothing that I can say can convince my hon. friend, but I will place him face to face with a statement which came not long ago from his own side of the House. My hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder), whom I regret not to see in his seat to-day, has a well deserved reputation in this House for being a shrewd and keen observer of what is going on in the country. Lately he addressed himself to this situation, and, within the hearing of my hon. friend, made the statement that agricultural production is in many respects not equal to the demand now pressing upon it. His words were:
The right hon. gentleman must realize that Canada is not producing the quantity of dairy produce that we might expect from it, an agricultural country. How can we justify this? Just last winter a gentleman sat down to his breakfast in the city of Ottawa and he had for his breakfast eggs from Russia, potatoes from Ireland, bacon from Denmark and butter from New Zealand.
Then the hon. member added pathetically:
That should not happen in this country.
On that list there was not one article of Canadian produce; it all came from abroad. No wonder that the hon. member for Dundas added pathetically, almost despairingly, that that should not happen in this country; but it has happened in this country; and it is happening at this moment. 'Tis true; 'tis a pity; and a pity 'tis, 'tis true. The hon. member for Dundas, who is a practical man, was not satisfied with pointing to the evil; he also suggested the remedy and immediately added these significant words:
That should not happen in this country. There is only one remedy and that is to get the people on the land.
These words were spoken within the hearing of my hon. friend the Minister of 'Finance, but what is there in his Budget to get the people on the land? There is not a trace of a thought in any word of his
[Sir Wilfrid Laurier.)
speech towards that object. This is the situation. My hon. friend the member for Dundas dilated upon what he had stated, and he made the statement and gave the proof also that in the last ten years the number of dairy animals had decreased in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island. Every one knows that the milch cow is the wealth of the farmer. We may have increased our wealth otherwise, but in that respect we have been losing wealth to a large extent in Ontario. According *to the figures given by the hon. member for Dundas, there was in the last decade, a decrease in milch cows of 33,784 in Ontario; 14,691 in Quebec; 2,552 in New Brunswick; 9,515 in Prince Edward Island, and 2,484 in Nova Scotia, a total of 63,026, Therefore at this moment, that particular form of wealth is decreasing and not increasing. The hon. member for Dundas might have gone farther and added that not only in dairy produce but in almost every other form of production the eastern provinces have not been keeping pace with the wants and requirements of the population. He might have modified his language and stated that the remedy for the situation is not only to get the people on the land, but that in the eastern provinces, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island, the effort and the duty of the Government should be to get the people back on the land. It is a fact that at this moment the land is deserted, and that we have not now in the eastern provinces the same number of tillers of the soil that we had ten years ago. This is the problem which was facing my hon. friend. I do not charge the Government with the responsibility; I do not say it is the fault of the Government that this is the state of affairs to-day, but I charge them with the responsibility for their failure to deal with the situation which is staring them in the face. They cannot plead that they are not responsible; what are they in office for? What are the pledges they have given to the people? Their pledges were pledges of reform, so as to make the people more prosperous, but instead of being more prosperous the people are less prosperous than they were. I charge the Government with failure of duty at least in not attempting to relieve the situation.
It is a fact of which everybody is
aware that in every civilized portion of the world there is a tendency for the rural population to desert

the land and to flock into the cities. In this respect Canada is not peculiar bat suffers in common with every other land. There are general oases which affect the rural population everywhere, but also there are special causes almost everywhere which are peculair to the country, and which can be remedied by legislation. As to the general causes, I say frankly, that probably they also may be remedied; but as to the particular causes it is certainly possible to remedy these if we apply ourselves to the work. Sir, in Great Britain to-day population is leaving the land and flocking to the cities. The causes there are largely to be found in the vicious land laws, the remnant of the old feudal system, which they aTe trying to remedy. These efforts that are being made in that country to remedy, if possible, these old vicious laws and win back the people to the land, is a spectacle to arouse our admiration. But in this country we have no feudal tenure, thank the Lord! We are free from that evil, but still we are not keeping our population on the land. And if we are to seek a remedy for this lamentable condition of affairs, that remedy, as I shall presently show, is to be sought in the direction of an expansion of trade.
Such is the situation in the eastern provinces, and as to the western provinces we must always remember the primary factor that in those provinces there are 150,000,000 acres of land ready for the tiller. Of these lands only 18,000,000 acres are today under culture, leaving 132,000,000 acres of as fertile land as there is in any part of the globe, and yet, as my hon. friend knows, we are making no headway towards increasing the settlement of that country. My hon. friend in his speech the other day rejoiced that our immigration is keeping up its volume. Here are his words:
It is gratifying to know not only that the stream of new settlers continues to flow into the Dominion, but that there is also apparent from year to year a marked improvement in the class arriving due to restrictive regulations.
I take issue with my hon. friend upon this statement. True, the volume of immigration is not decreasing, it is keeping up as before; but the hon. gentleman is in error when he speaks of ' new settlers.' They are not new settlers for the land tha.t are coming in at the present time, but rather mechanics and artisans. At the present moment, as he knows, the number of people who settle on the land, and the acreage of land which goes under cultivation are decreasing year by year. In 1910-11, the homestead entries, pre-emptions, purchased homesteads and South African veteran homesteads were 63,830; in 1911-12, they were 52,553; in 1912-13, 43,552; and foT the year just ended the number was only 38,856. So, they are not new settlers who are coming in, but rather a different class of immigrants. The immigrants we desire in this country are farmers, farm labourers and domestic servants and instead of these we are getting artisans and mechanics who find no work and simply drift into the cities to swell the ranks of the growing army of the unemployed.
We are beyond all an agricultural country. But, if agriculture is at a standstill, there is a blemish upon the country lo which nobody can close his eyes, and that is the situation at the present time. For this situation there must be a cause. If in the older provinces, the people leave the land and flock to the cities, if in the new provinces the tillers of the soil no longer go upon the soil, then there must be some cause for it. Of course, a3 this question has been more than gnce debated in this House, various opinions have been expressed upon it. There may be occasion for honest differences of opinion; but there are men who are in a position to give us information upon the subject and whose opinion is more valuable than the opinion of any others, and they are the farmers of this country. The farmers who have been heard more than once, before the Government have stated what are the causes which have produced this result, and they have pointed out the remedy. So far as I have been able to inform myself by reading their memorial, those causes are two: first, the high cost of production and the next the insufficiency of markets. As to the high cost of production, more than once, and with unanimous voice, the farmers have declared what they wanted and have suggested the remedy which would afford them relief. They asked to have agricultural implements free from taxation. We have heard this question debated in this House more than once and have heard many opinions expressed upon it. When the farmer asks that the tools of his occupation should be free from taxation,, that they should not be made heavier in his hands than they naturally are, nobody can say that is an unfair demand. Everybody, whether he sits on this side of the House dr on that would agree with me that this is a perfectly natural demand, and one

which ought to be granted unless there is a paramount reason to the contrary.
It has been asserted on the floor of this House during this debate that the hardships which the settlers of the prairies suffer do not compare with the hardships which our forefathers in this part of Canada had to undergo when hewing out for themselves and their families homes out of the forest. I am disposed to agree with'that: I believe that the hardships of the men of the prairies to-day, are not to be compared with those of our forefathers in this part of Canada. But, Sir, because we can do nothing for the dead, is that reason why we should refuse help for the living? I believe it to be true that the settlers of the West do not suffer as great hardships as did those of a generation past in this section of the country; but, Sir, if it is in our power to remove from the tiller of the soil to-day a part of the burden which he has to carry, why should we not apply ourselves to it? The hardships of today affe not as great as were those of the past; but, Sir, there are hardships to-day also. There are members in this House who have in their desks letters from settlers of the western prairies enclosing notice sent from the agent of the implement maker telling the settler that unless his account is paid it will be collected by the sheriff. Such letters I have seen myself. It is a oruel hardship when a man i3 subject to such treatment; and if it be in my power to diminish and minimize this evil in any way, I will take the risk of attempting it whatever be the consequence to myself. Bit, when the farmers came to the Government and asked that their implements be relieved from taxation, the answer was that it could not be done. And what was the reason ? The reason given was that free implements means free trade. And, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is responsible for that sentiment. It is a sentence to which he gave utterance evidently with some satisfaction, because he repeated it on more than one occasion in the course of his Budget speech, as well as in his speech on the Address. The Minister of Finance says that not only free implements, but that free food also, means free trade. I ask my hon. friend what does he mean by saying that free implements would mean free trade ? I say to him in all frankness, as friend to friend, that his expression is neither fact nor metaphor, it is loose and illogical. Free implements in 1914 mean free trade no more than did free

lumber in 1893 or 1894, granted under a Conservative Government. I tell my hon. friend the catch phrase * free implements means free trade ' is an appeal to the prejudice which we know exists in certain parts of this country against the very idea of freedom of trade. Even in this House the very mention of free trade is met by derisive laughter and jeers from hon. gentlemen on the other side. After all, Mr. Speaker, whatever may be the opinion on this side or the other side as to the benefits of free trade, it cannot be denied that there is only one country in the world today which has free trade, and that is the country which of all others, has shown itself above any other in commerce, in finance, and in the art and science of government In the fields of human speculation and human thought there are other nations which maintain supremacy over England. Germany is certainly ahead of England and of all other nations in philosophic research. I think that for precision and grace in literature, France can claim unmatched excellence. But in commerce, in finance, and in the art and science of government, the nation does not exist, and never has existed, which can compare with Great Britain-the mother of freedom of thought and of civil and commercial liberty. It seems to me, in view of the fact that that great nation has emerged from her protective policy of years, to a conception of the value of free trade, that the least hon. members can do is to reflect that perhaps there is something in free trade which has never been dreamed of in their philosophy.
The application of economic principles is not to be determined simply from theoretical conceptions. We on this side of the House; we, the Liberals of Canada, while we have upheld the cause of free trade-
Oh, oh.

We have
always contended that the policy best suited to this country is not a protective tariff but a customs tariff for revenue purposes. I am well aware-and this is evidenced by the jeers which I heard a moment ago-that I have been taken to task in this debate and in many other debates for what is termed my economic and fiscal inconsistencies.
Some hem. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

I observe that I have struck a responsive chord in hon. gentlemen opposite. I have been accused Off having been at one time in favour of commercial union and of I do not know

how many other different heresies. The House is aware, Sir, that I never answered any such charges, not because I do not fully appreciate the courtesy and honour which was offered me by bringing my poor person into prominence, but because I never thought that my poor person was worthy of the honour of taking up so much of the time of the House. But there is one man in this House whom I will not allow to take such liberties with the truth, and that is my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. He knows that these assertions are not true; he knows that if they were true he would not for so long have pulled an oar in the boat of which I was in charge, and in which he and I together had to face, and to successfully plough through many an angry billow. The time came, however, when my hon. friend changed his mind. This is a free country, and he had a right to do so. Of course I am sorry-sorry for myself, but more sorry for him, because if any one changed his mind or his politics it was not I, but my hon. friend.
When we came into office in 1896 we found a protective tariff in force. A protective tajriff creates a factitious atmosphere, capital is invested and new industries are started and if you incautiously interfere with that tariff you may produce a financial crisis or a commercial panic which may bring serious disaster to the country. We had that in view; we have it in view yet. The Democrats of the United States, when they came into office two years ago, had the same thing in view; they did not tear the tariff all to pieces at once; they had to proceed cautiously so as not to do injustice to any class and so as to give relief to the consumers without hurting the manufacturers. I think I can say that in 1896 we ourselves did the same thing; we were able to give relief to the consumers and did no injury to any of the manufacturers. But to-day we are told a different story. When we brought in our tariff in 1896 we were at once told on the floor of this House that we would destroy the industries of Canada. As time went on and it was found that the tariff suited the needs of the people; and had produced a period of unexampled prosperity, the tune was changed and we were charged with having kept the tariff in its entirety. I say that there is as much truth in the one statement as there is in the other. When we are told by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that we did nothing to reform the tariff, let me remind them that we took the duty off many articles used by the farmer. We removed the duty upon binder twine, upon barbed wire and upon 180
cordage. We did more than that. When we introduced the Iritish preference we introduced a principle the effect of which is felt to this day. We introduced the British preference cautiously. We first reduced the duty on imports from the British Empire by 124 per cent, then by 25 per cent, and finally by 334 per cent of the general tariff; and the result has been that the British preference has kept the price of articles in this country, both those manufactured in Canada and those imported even from the United States, at a reasonable level, because it is a fact that while manufactured goods imported from the United States have to pay the general duty, the price to the consumer is fixed iby the price of articles imported under the British preference. We introduced a new principle the effect of which to-day is enormous. My friend Mr. Paterson, of lamented memory, said once, and I believe with perfect truth, that if the importations of 1911 had been under the tariff of 1896, the Government would have taken from the consumer of this country something like $8,000,000 more than we did take. Therefore, this is our justification for the policy which we adopted, the policy which we maintain and the policy which we propose to apply on the present occasion.
Now, Sir, we propose to deal with farming implements as with everything. else Is the duty on farm implements required for revenue purposes? Nobody will pretend that. Then, can the duty be taken off without any injury to the manufacturer of implements? I have yet to learn tha under present conditions the manufacturers of implements in Canada cannot compete with the American manufacturer in the home market. We know that he competes with the American manufacturer in England, in France, in Germany, in Hungary and in many other countries. If the Canadian manufacturer can meet his American competitor in England, or in France, or in Germany, or in Hungary, is there any reason why he cannot meet him on the soil of Canada? An objection has been made for which there is some ground, in that it has been said that it is not fair to remove the duty from the manufactured article because there is a duty upon the raw material. There may be something in that, but I believe that it is a sufficient answer to say that upon everything except coal there is as much duty upon the raw material in the United States, as there is



in Canada, and if there is as much duty on one side as on the other there is a parity of manufacturing conditions and the objection does not hold. As to coal, there may be an argument, but it is a notorious fact that coal is being gradually, nay rapidly, replaced by electrical energy. 'If, after all, these different elements cannot be conciliated, if we have to make the choice between one and the other, whatever may be the position taken by our friends on the other side of the House I say for my part; if we have to make a choice between one interest and the other interest I stand by the agricultural industry which, in the language of my hon. friend, is the basis of all industries, without which no other industry can flourish.
Then, Sir, we come to the other request which has been made by the farmers. They have represented that they are hampered by the cost of production; and that they are still more hampered by the insufficiency of markets. If there is one thing to-day which the farmers want, especially the western farmers, it is wider markets for their products. Their demand has been denied, rudely denied I may say. But there is one thing which the farmers have been given without asking for it and given with a plenteous hand; they have been given advice. The advice is given to them from all quarters on the other side of the House;	' Why don't you go into mixed
farming? ' How many times have we heard that during the present debate? It can be depended upon that the western farmers will go into mixed farming as soon as they find it more profitable than wheat raising. But we have the experience of the past all over this continent to show that on new soil, whether prairie soil or forest soil, the crop mostprofitableto the farmer has been wheat. We can follow the production of wheat from the earliest days of the discovery of this continent until the present time; first of all the New England states, in the province of Quebec, in the province of Ontario, in the Genesee valley, then in the state of Illinois, in the state of Minnesota; until now at last it is centered in the three prairie provinces of Canada. As soon as it is profitable for the farmer to go into mixed farming he will do it, but in the meantime he grows wheat. Last year he grew 200,-nno,000 bushels of wheat. Where is that wheat to go? At present he has only two markets, the home market and the English market. How much can the home market consume? Not 50,000,000 bushels. It is known from statistics that the proportion 
of consumption is five bushels per head of population, and therefore not 50,000,000 bushels will be taken by the home market. Up to the present moment the English market has not taken more than 50,000,000 bushels and where is the rest to go? The farmers of the West has to find a market for it somewhere. You tell him he cannot send his wheat to the United States, but even now he sends his wheat to the United States in spite of all obstacles. In the last two or three months of the last fiscal year, 2,000,000 bushels of grain were sent from Canada into the United States in the face of an adverse duty. But we are told by hon. gentlemen opposite: It is no use to try to open the markets of the United States to the western growers of wheat because the Americans are themselves exporters 'of wheat. What a fallacy. The Americans are growers of wheat, it is true; but they are not growers of our wheat and they must have it. Everybody knows that for the last ten years, more perhaps, but certainly for the last ten years, the American people have imported our wheat in bond to grind it in their mills for the European market? What the Americans are doing for the European market they will have to do for their own market also. We are told that the farmers of the West do not know their own business. At all events we can trust to them that they understand this question as well as their critics, and the monopolists who tell them that they do not know anything of their business and that they have a monopoly of intelligence as well as a monopoly of markets. There is another reason which 1 was surprised to hear advanced upon the floor of this House during this very debate. We have been told: Beware of the Americans; there is a sinister intent in their tariff to-day. The Americans have revised their tariff. Their new tariff provides that wheat shall be free from all countries except those having a tariff against their wheat and wheat products. We have been told: Beware, there is a sinister intent in this. I have only this to say, that the present American tariff is the direct inspiration 'f President Woodrow Wilson, and I do not hesitate to say, and everybody will agree with me, that with the advent of Mr. Wilson a new page has been turned in American history. If there was a time when it could be charged against American tariff legislation that it was hostile, you cannot charge that to the legislation which is inspired by Mr. Wilson; you cannot charge it against a man who to-day is risking his own popularity amongst his own party to keep intact the honour of the American people, to mainr

tain sacred international obligations, and to give to the trade of the world equal treatment with American trade upon a canal built with American money.
When hon. gentlemen charge there is hostile design in that tariff which was the inspiration of President Wilson, I say that such charges fail to reach the man against whom they are directed, and recoil to the confusion and shame of those who make them.
Against the removal of the duty on wheat, I have heard only one argument which has made the slightest impression on my mind, and that is the complaint of Canadian millers. Upon this subject, however, I speak with some diffidence because I do not profess to be competent to discuss the technicalities of this matter; but I have yet to learn from anything that come before me that the Canadian millers are not on a footing of equality with American millers either in the Canadian or the American market. I have not been able to discover what advantage the American miller would have over the Canadian miller if we had the American market? My belief is that the millers on the Canadian side of the St. Lawrence-on the Welland canal and on the Lachine canal-can capture the market of New York against the Mississippi Valley millers because of their advantage in greater proximity to that market. I have nothing further to say on this point except, as I said a moment ago in reference to agricultural implements, that, if the two interests cannot be reconciled, and if we have to choose between them, I stand for the basic industry of this country and without which no other industry can flourish. That is the situation so far as one part of the question is concerned.
All the requests of the farmers have been met with a deaf ear and stern refusals, and as to the consumers the Government has not given them even a passing thought. When Parliament met some three months ago, the very first thing we, on this side, did, was to call the attention of the Government to the high cost of living. We did not press the Government, but we put them on [DOT]their guard by asking them to look into the matter and to provide some measure of relief. Our suggestion met with a very cold reception, and the Government has evidently remained callous up to this moment. If they are not impressed with the conditions in Canada as to the high cost of living they [DOT]are the only people in this Dominion who are not. Some days ago I read a lecture on thiis question by Professor Osborne of Mani-1801
toba University, and coming from such a source, you may well imagine that his opinions are not influenced by
4 p.m. party politics, his lecture being a mere economic discussion of the problem. This is how he opened:
That the cost of living In Canada to-day is exorbitant, there can be no question. The fact is in evidence on every hand. We see signs of it in every newspaper. A commission of investigation has been appointed in one quarter, an angry league of consumers is being formed in another, and the general pubuc may be said to be in a state of revolt on the question. A recent British investigation shows that the cost of living in Canada has increased fifty-one per cent in twelve years. Its nearest competitor in this regard shows an increase of only thirty-nine per cent. The condition has emerged finally in the appointment of a commission by the Government of Canada, but the best evidence of the fact lies in the struggle the large proportion of our population is waging in order to make ends meet. The number of dependents in our own midst is evidently alarmingly on the increase. Ten thousand free dinners are reported to have been given in Winnipeg on Christmas Day. It is admirable that the dinners should be given, but it is a shame that the majority of them should have had to be.
Who will dispute that? I am sorry I cannot give his arguments or statistics, but the conclusion to which he came was that if the cost of living is high, it is not because the producer is paid an abnormal price, but because of enormous profits that go into the pockets of combines and trusts. Speaking of the high cost of food, in so far as that high cost means higher profits for the farmer, nobody makes any objection. The price of food-stuffs commenced to increase some fifteen years ago when we had the commencement of that period of prosperity which synchronized-to, use the word of my hon. friend-with the coming to power of the late Administration, and with defeat of which the disappearance of prosperity also synchronized. Prices increased in those fifteen years, but everybody was satisfied that the farmer should get higher prices for his products. Times have changed; there are hard times now. Prices are just as high as they were, the difference is that they are going into the pockets of combines and trusts and not into the pockets of the farmers. Trusts and combines are the bane of these latter days. They are everywhere, but especially in protected countries, where they seem to find a congenial habitat, just as do microbes in dirt and darkness. In the United States they have combines in milk, in meat, in bread, in sugar, in all kinds of commodi-

ties, and Canada is following suit at a pretty lively rate. We have combines in meat, in bread and in flour. Bacon is an article of daily consumption, to toe found on the table of every consumer, and to-day bacon is sold to the consumer in England at 14J cents per pound, while in Toronto, Montreal and all the western cities of Canada it is sold for 191 cents per pound, or five cents more than in England. That five cents does not go into the pockets of the farmer, but into the pockets of the combine. So it is with flour. To-day flour sells in Canada for something like $5.50 per barrel, and in England the same flour sells for $4.70. These differences in price do not go into the pockets of the farmer, but into the pockets of the combines. I will be told -I am sure of it-that prices in England are lower because wages are low in England, while wages in Canada are high. I will be told that in England the working man is paid a starvation wage, but that in Canada he is paid such a wage that he can bring up his family in comfort and respectability. When it was suggested to the Minister of Finance that we might haVe free food, he at once objected with horror, and he said it could not be done, because in Canada we wanted to keep the wages of our artisans and our workmen up to the fair wage standard.
These are !his very words. Then he gave a concrete example. He said some time ago, in answer to myself, that he could not think of having free food because free food would afleot prejudicially some 7,000 establishments and the wages of some 50,000 operatives. I had better quote the words of my hon. friend on this point:
In addition to that, free food means that the policy of my right hon. friend affects in Canada, according to the statistics of the Tear Book, 6,985 establishments with a capital of $133,000,000, employing 52,000 men on wages, paying $14,000,000 in wages every year, using material to the amount of $175,000,000, and with an output of $245,000,000.
These are high sounding words. The figures sound big, but analyse them, and they are perfectly hollow. The reason my hon. friend says he cannot think of having free food is because if we were to attempt it we would affect the wages of 52,000 men who earn something like $14,000,000. How much is that for each one of these 52,000 men? What does it represent? It would mean for each $270 a year or $5.20 a week. That is the standard which my hon. friend says must toe kept up in the interest of the operatives of the country. Is my

hon. friend serious? Here are his own words, the statement and the figures which he gave-$14,000,000 divided among 52,000, operatives and it means $270 a year for each one of these operatives upon which to bring up his family in comfort and respectability.
What becomes of the theory of my hon. friend ? Delusion ! Oh, delusion it is. The theory that taxation increases wages is not justified, at least for the kind of products to which my hon. friend refers. Are we to be told that we are going to continue to pay two and three prices for food in order to have such wages as $270 a year? This is the condition to which my hon. friend has reference. It has been written that truth and justice will in the end prevail. Truth and justice have already come. When the prophet Balaam was called upon to curse the people he met in his path the angel of the LoTd, and in spite of himself he had to bless instead of curse. My hon. friend met in his path the angel of. truth, and from his own words he blessed where he wanted to curse, and he cursed where he wanted to bless.
We have in this country a condition of things that is a cause of anxiety to every wage-earner and to every mother of a family. But we have been told that this thing is to be preserved intact because if we touched it we would affect the wages of the operatives of Canada. Many people believed, and I am sure that hon. members on the other side of the House believed, that working men were paid a high wage, that they were getting $600, or $700 or $800 a year, but they are only getting $270 a year, and you have it from the mouth of the Minister of Finance.
In the face of such a condition, these figures teach a lesson and that lesson is that there is a great deal of fallacy in the theory which has long been prevalent, that taxation means high wages. These figures show clearly that it does not, and it is time-high time-that we should revise the tariff with a view of reducing the cost of living and relieving the wage-earners, and the mothers who have to bring up families upon this meagre income, from the incubus which has been upon them night and day, and which is a disgrace to the fair name of Canada.
We on this side of the House are not revolutionists; we are reformers, but we tell hon. gentlemen opposite that the tariff exists for the people and not the people for the tariff. The tariff is not immutable

like the laws of the Medes and Persians. The tariff has to be readjusted from time to time to bring it into harmony with changed conditions. It has to be readjusted periodically, because after the lapse of a certain period we know that changes in conditions have taken place and the tariff has to be readjusted in order to correct errors and to remove evil where evil exists.
But, I may be told that the tariff is of my own creation. The tariff was of our own creation; it suited the year 1897, but eighteen years have passed since and the time has come when we must have a revision in order to correct errors and to meet changed conditions. We were told the other day by the Minister of Finance that he was ready for and invited the challenge. We on this side of the House accept the challenge upon this one question, and, animated with the view that the time has'eome for a new revision of the tariff, I beg to call the attention of the House to this proposition, which I move;
That this House is of opinion that in view of the prevailing economic conditions of the country it is advisable to place wheat, wheat products, and agricultural implements on the free list; and that without doing injustice to any class, steps should be taken to alleviate the high cost of living by considerate removal of taxation.
Hon. GEORGE E. FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):	Mr. Speaker, at
this particular period of the debate, when the ground has ibeen very well gone over and everything winnowed out, it is not to be wondered at if my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who has just spoken, or that I, who am to follow him, should find it very difficult indeed to get enough material upon which to base a speech.
I do not know that I could in any more humane way let down my right hon. friend on the words which have just been uttered by him, and he will probably be in a position to return the compliment to me when I have made my few remarks. Two courses are open to me; one, make a review of the situation, the other to devote my attention to the remarks made by the preceding speaker and make as fair an answer as I can to him. Should I take the latter course, I am quite conscious, if I do it properly and do it tersely, that it will not be necessary for me to take up much of the time of the House; should I take the other, I am afraid I will have to trespass upon the patience of both sides of the House, and be open to the imputation of having left the remarks of my right hon. friend unanswered. Therefore, if the House will allow me, I will say a few words with reference to the remarks of my right hon. friend.
The motion moved by the right hon. gentleman is not quite so inclusive as many people in this country had been led to believe it would be. I remember reading a speech made by my Tight hon. friend in the city of Hamilton in which he took very much broader grounds than he takes today ; grounds in which he covered the necessities of the occasion as he saw them, in far more vigorous English than he has used here to-day. What has taken place which has reduced the broad, wide platform of my right hon. friend enunciated: as the foreword and motto from this time-on of the party that he leads? What has necessitated the paring down of that wider ground to the far narrower limits in which he has confined it to-day? I think we, who have been observers of what has been taking place, quite well understand some of the reasons why the motion of my right hon. friend is so inadequate to his lofty and wide professions. Perhaps my right hon. friend knows more about these reasons than I do; but 1 am inclined to think that none of us will be far away from a proper conclusion, if we arrive at a solution of this little problem somewhat in this way, that my right hon. friend leads a heterogeneous *army made up of many small battalions, each battalion being almost limited to the leader of the same, he being both the leader and the battalion itself. My right hon. friend has had difficulties facing him for the last three weeks, if not longer, and he has tried to cut the Gordian knot by putting on the table of the House a resolution in which he and his party-after all they have said, after all their declamations, after all their professions, after all their vehement assertions as to the cost of food products and as to the necessity for giving the homes of this country something cheaper in the way of food-stand for free wheat and free agricultural implements, but not for free food. That is not as broad a gage of battle as the Minister of Finance invited him to throw down. We certainly have the advantage on this side of being broader gauged in that respect and it is no doubt a disappointment to the Minister of Finance, as it is to all of us, that the field of battle has been brought down from a high and broad series of plains and hills, where you could have deployed in splendid style and carried on the battle in

not to lecture them. If hon. gentlemen on this side give their views, that is what men in this House are here for. The business of public men is to get the best information that they can and to give to the public the best information that they can after they get it; to interchange their views, one with another, for the common benefit and for the common interest.	Our advice to the western
farmer to go into mixed farming, which has been scouted by hon. gentlemen opposite, is the very thing which is taking hold of the West to-day from one end to the other. In all organizations in the West; in all bankers' meetings; in the meetings of any society; in all the agricultural associations and agricultural papers, the burden of the song, the advice and the counsel to-day is: We must change our methods and get into mixed farming. Why should we be objurgated because we express the same opinion here? What we are trying to do and what we ought to try to do in this House is to give the best information that we can and to interchange our views for the good of the country. I have no hesitation in saying that in this time of readjustment-for it is a time of readjustment all through the country-one of the biggest things in readjustment is that which is taking place in our great West to-day, and that readjustment is on the line of less exclusive wheat production for the sake of the sale of the wheat, and for more variety of industry and production in the West.
What my right hon. friend and his followers on the other side of the House are agreed upon is the assertion that this is a period of depression in Canada. There is no lack of unanimity among them in that respect. Some of them are so set upon having this little idea all to themselves that they resent any attempt on our part to show that there is any similar depression in some other country. This they vigorously deny; the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) was very wrathy in the thought that any one should suggest that any other country should have a bit of this depression at this particular time. He wants it all for Canada, and especially he wants it all for the West. We will agree, for the sake of peace and Quietness, that this is a time of depression as compared with the buoyancy of the past in the Dominion of Canada. But I take leave to point out what I think has already been pointed out: That there are many features of this so-called depression 
in Canada that are worth keeping in mind. What are they ? That after a period of unexampled expansion, extending over a long period of years, with very little break,
all the indicia of progress and virility and power are pretty nearly as striking to-day as they were in 1912 or 1913. Your revenue, which is an index of the business that is done, is $163,000,000 for the year which has just ended; only $6,000,000 less than it was in 1912. Turn again to another indication -the trade of the country. After an unexampled series of brilliant and progressive trade years, 1913 shows you a trade which is greater than 1912 by $200,000,000, and which is well up to, if not in advance of, the trade of 1912-13. But you go still further than that; you go down to what are the foundations upon which the nation rests

its great basic productive industries-and what do you find ? I believe that when the figures for 1913-14, marked by the depression so dearly loved and so expatiated upon by our friends opposite, are totalled up you will find that in our basic industries we have reached the largest output in the history of the country. You will find that our mines will show as compared with 1912 for 1914 some $14,000,000 worth 6i extra output, and you will find that our manufactures will show $20,000,000 extra output. You will find that our fisheries will show $4,000,000; that our forests will show $3,000,000; that our animal products will show $6,000,000; our agricultural products $101,000,000 and, as I said, our manufactured products, $20,000,000. Can you go back to any other period of the history of Canada or of any other country and show a silver lining like that to the depression which was upon the surface of the cloud? It cannot be found in Canada, it cannot be found anywhere else. That is in all the depressions you talk about in the very year in which you talk about it, all these great basic industries are producing by millions more than they did in any other year in the history of our Canadian nation. The depression is not a sign of inherent weakness; it is more like the case of a man of super-abundant energy who, for a time, has been putting forth superhuman exertions and is tired and his nerve force and his bodily vigour are somewhat dulled for the time being. All you need to do is to give him a rest and put him on a fair regime for a little while; the man's inherent vigour and vitality will break forth in still greater effort and be crowned with still greater results. A depression like that I am not going to lament over, and I present that

kind of a depression to my hon. friends for their sustenance and their comfort. It is perhaps not just the kind they would like, but it is the only one that the country can give them at the present time, and they will have to be content with it.
My right hon. friend thought he made a great point in proving that agriculture was on the decline by the declaration that there had been a diminution in homestead entries in the West during the last few years. But my right hon. friend, if he had gone back a (little earlier than that, would have found that these things are apt to occur; they are not inherent signs of decadence or of a downward tendency, they are a temporary thing, which, in the very mutations of social and national progress, always vary the landscape, sometimes throwing a shade of darkness, at other times breaking out into splendid light. From 1906 to 1908 in his time, homestead entries went down by 11,000. In the last period that he has quoted they went down by about 11,000. As a matter of fact about 600 less than in the preceding period to which I have alluded. Well it is worth while calling it to mind that I did not hear my right hon. friend in 1908 talking about the decadence of agriculture and proving it by the fact' that homestead entries in those two years had gone down by about 11,000.
I want to ask my right hon. friend a question. As leader of the Opposition, putting forth the facts upon which he based his case, has he been certain that the facts are correct? I allude to just one point. He was talking about the millers and the flour industry, and made the statement that flour sold in Canada for $5.50 per barrel, and was selling, in London and Liverpool for $4.70. Where does my right hon. friend get these statistics and that information? We had a statement made by the hon. member for South Cape Breton the other day which .conveyed a double inaccuracy. He declared, in order to make a point against the millers and to curry favour with the consumers, that flour was sold for $5.10 in Montreal, and that down in Halifax you had to pay $6.50 for it. That is a .strange statement when you come to think of it. The freight from Montreal to Halifax is exactly 25 cents a barrel; 25 cents added to $5.10 would make $5.35. I never believed that the Halifax people were so bereft of business acumen and ability as to pay $6.50 there for flour which they could have got in Montreal for $5.10 and carted down by the Intercolonial for 25 cents. He made the statement also
that flour which sold for $5.10 in Montreal was .sold in London for $4.18. My right hon. friend, wherever he got his information, was sadly out. He was not? Well,
I am not going to quarrel about the adjective, but I am bound to maintain that he was far out. I hold here the actual statistics and the prices of. flour in the different months. Canada spring patents in January are quoted in Liverpool at from $6.33 to $6.81. All through the month of January they ran about those even quotations. In February the .same quotations were followed pretty closely, $6.33 to $6.81, and the other patents in varying degrees.
Per barrel?
Per barrel.
Is flour sold in barrels in England?
It is sold in bags, and there are so many bags to the barrel, and the price here is the barrel price.
The hon. gentleman may be right, but he should not be too sure about it.
I think I am so .sure that I cannot help but be right. The Liverpool price is quoted on the, basis of a sack containing 280 lbs.
How many pounds in a sack?
So long as my hon. friend and myself are going to have a little tilt about .sacks, I am going to tell him that there are several kinds of sacks.
You would make a good .sheep farmer.
I would like to ask my hon. friend if he can answer a conundrum. Why are there more black sheep in Nova Scotia than white ones?
The hon. gentleman is .so efficient in his knowledge of sacks that I thought he would also be proficient in reference to sheep.

If my hon. friend wants to get to the facts, the price quotation is based on 280 lbs., which may be all contained in one .sack. There are sacks that have 98 lbs., and sacks that run to 280 lbs., and sacks that contain 112 lbs. They run so many stone to the sack. As I stated before, the price is reduced to the barrel basis of 280 lbs.

Is it higher
in England than in Canada?'
Yes, for that kind.

I do not think
the figures from which the hon. gentleman is quoting reduced the cost from sacks to weight in barrels.

If they are not reduced
from the sack to the barrel, then they are reduced to the sack price for 280 pounds. You can figure out the difference and you will still find that I am on the right side of the equation, and that the wrong figures have not been given.

Withdraw the
statement about prices, and go ahead.
I will tell you what I will do: I will look at it again.

The hon.
minister challenges my figures. I do not pretend to be an expert myself, but in some correspondence in the newspaper the other day I saw the statement that the price of flour in England is lower than in Canada.
I asked a friend to look into the matter- he is a very careful man, and I rely on his authority-and this is the information he sent me. He gives the price of flour in Toronto, Winnipeg, Montreal and London, England, for the month of April in the years 1912, 1913 and 1914. In 1912, the prices were:	Toronto, $5.30; Winnipeg, $5.70;
Montreal, $5.50; London, $4.95. In 1913, Toronto, $5.10; Winnipeg, $5.70; Montreal, $5.20; London, $5.04. In 1914, Toronto, $5.30; Winnipeg, $5; Montreal, $5.40, and London, $4.70.
