speechtext: I would like to say to my right hon. friend that I was present when a delegation of millers from different parts of the country presented their views to the Government, and I put that very question to them. I said that it had been stated in the public press that flour was sold abroad at a lower price than in Canada, and they assured me that that was not the case. I have no personal knowledge of the facts, but they said the flour sold abroad at lower prices was of a quality that could not be sold in Canada.
I do not know personally, but I got the information from a man on whom I can rely.

Change the figures to
$4.40 a barrel and you will be all right.

These little difficulties occur because the question has not been carefully studied beforehand. This was put in my hands just before I came in. I had the impression that the prices I have read were reduced to the barrel basis, but looking at it again I find that they are reduced to the 280 pound sack basis; so that you would have to take that proportion off from the $6.33 to the $6.81 to get at the barrel price, That would bring it to $4.80.

The question remains as to whether the prices which my right hon. friend has read are for the same grades of flour or not. That is the point. I have the best information I can get. I have here a list of the different grades of flour which I propose to give to the House: first of all, there is the top patent; then the second patent or bakers' flour; then first clear and second clear. The top patent is the highest grade of flour, and of that grade very little, if any, is exported to the old country. I think I am correct in my facts up to that. The second patent is a flour which is used by bakers, and a very small proportion of that grade is exported to the old country. In the month of January, for instance, only about 36 per cent of the total product of that kind of flour was exported. The kind of flour exported to Great Britain is the first clear. That is a strong dark flour which is almost Unsaleable in Canada. Our householders use only top patent flour, and the bakers use second patent, so that when you say flour costs the householder in Toronto $5.10 or $5.18 and sells at Liverpool or London at $4.18 or $4.20, you have got to be certain that you have your grades of flour lined up properly, because in all probability you are comparing first clear in the London or Liverpool market with top or second patent in the Canadian market.
The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) said that Britain took only the best grade of flour, and so he came to the conclusion that the flour quoted in London at $4.18 compared with the flour sold in Montreal or Toronto at $5.10 or $5.18.

No, I did not say that.
I said the very best flour was used for export, and that the statement that only the worst grades of flour were exported to England was incorrect. I gave statements to show that the very same kind of flour selling for $5.50 in Montreal costs only $4.18 in Liverpool.

My hon. friend will find that he is wrong in that. 1
5 p-m. think he was challenged lor his authority, and he stated that he read from a statement in the Montreal Standard by a correspondent who did not attach his name. I am quite certain that if he will go to the proper sources of information he will find he is mistaken in saying that the best grades of flour aire exported to the old country. The opposite is the fact; it is the low grade flour that is exported to the old country. Of the first clear grade, about 90 per cent is exported to the old country, and but 10 per cent used in this country. Of the second clear, 90 per cent goes to the old country, mostly for feed purposes, and but a small proportion is used in this country, also for feed purposes. We must distinguish the flour quoted at Montreal, Toronto, Halifax and St. John, which is always either top patent or second patent if it is for bakers' use, ot blended if it is a family flour, from the flour exported to the old country, which is of a quality that our people will not use.
Is not our export flour made from a blended wheat?
I am informed that blended flours are not exported from this country to any appreciable extent at the present time.
I understand that almost nothing else is exported at the present time.

My hon. friend will find that his information is not correct. After this digression on the technical point of the price of flours, I want to get back to my remarks in reference to the speech of my right hon. friend.
In talking about the influences which tend to attract people to the farms, the diversion from which was so much deplored by my right hon. friend, there are several which are working in the direction of attractions to the farm and the land. Amongst these influences none is greater than the question of good roads. In all
the foremost agricultural countries of the world, where they are striving to keep people on the farm and to attract them to the farm, the subject of good roads is receiving the greatest attention and in this connection large amounts of money are being expended. It is in that direction that much good is being done in the Dominion of Canada as well. But 1 would remind my right hon. friend that he has not been forward inhelpingthis present Government in its endeavour to have good roads constructed in the different provinces of the Dominion.
I believe that a forward policy on the question of good roads, carried out fully and carefully in the country, will do more than almost anything else to keep people upon the farms, to attract people to the farms and to make farming a more delightful and companionable occupation than it is at the present time.
In connection with that, good roads also includes electric railways and tramways and everything of that kind that can contribute to the quick carriage both of information and the products of the field from wqjeT^ they are produced to the centres of population where they are marketed. It is along that line that this Government has taken a forward step. My right hon. friend's party have not assisted this Government in aiding and helping the farmers in that direction in the way in which they should have done.
My right hon. friend had his play with my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, recalling the time some years ago when he and the Minister of Finance were paddling in the same canoe and he rather thinks it is to the disadvantage of the minister that he got out of that canoe. There are two remarks which I have to make in respect to that. When the Minister of Finance was paddling in the canoe with my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, honest now, was not the leader of the Opposition telling the Minister of Finance-not Minister of Finance at that time: Do not have any qualms of conscience; I am talking free trade where I want to get votes, but-whisper it in confidence-go paddling along in that same old canoe with me and I will take care of the manufacturers. And to use a word of my right hon, friend, there is a synchronization in time, as to when the Minister of Finance left that canoe, when he began to get very suspicious as to whether or not his right hon. friend was not playing double with him and when he thought discretion was the better part of valour and that the canoe should be

left. I do not think I shall follow my right hon. friend any farther along the line of his remarks hut shall take np some new subjects in the time that remains to me along more general lines and I will possibly touch on some things that my right hon. friend has said.
My right hon. friend is looking for a policy -I sympathize with him very much in the difficulties which surround him-and is trying to find a policy that is practical and that will carry with it some few shreds of consistency. My right hon. friend's position is a hard one. He was opposed to the National Policy from 1878 to 1896, opposed to it tooth and nail and with every resort in his power. He came into power in 1896 and, despite all his professions of hostility to protection and its methods, he espoused the protective principle, embalmed it in his tariff, kept it there against assaults from within his own ranks and assaults from without, and up to the time of the dissolution of Parliament he maintained that principle of avowed protection in his tariff. In 1911 he took up the idea of the reciprocity pact with the United States Government, and he ventured his fortunes upon that. He went to the country upon that issue. Never in the history of Canada was an issue more clearly put before the electorate than was that issue in 1911. Never was there a more intelligent discussion of a public question on the hustings than in August and September of that year. Never was there a more emphatic reply to the issue which was raised than the reply given by the electorate in September, 1911. My right hon. friend remembers that defeat and finds it very difficult to go back to the reciprocity issue of 1911. He is disinclined to go back to the protective policy which he carried into effect from 1896 to 1911. Why? Not perhaps because he does not think that it embodies the right principle but because it does not differentiate him sufficiently from the party in power and therefore it is of no effect in the country for him to espouse that principle. It is a political policy that he is after and not a policy for the country. '
If it were a policy for the country it would be one of two; either the policy that he carried out for fifteen years, that he gave the seal of his approval to and under which he declares this country progressed with immense strides, or it would be a repetition and recall of the policy of reciprocity as set forth by the party in 1911. But my right hon. friend finds this last impossible in face of the great revolt of the electors. He finds 
the first impossible because it gives him no line of cleavage with the party in power upon the great issue of the country-the fiscal issue. Therefore, he is bound to look for a political and party tariff question in order to make an issue before the electors. So he catches on to this cry, .the most patent and the easiest.
Who does not like to have beefsteak, fresh and juicy, put on his table at twelve cents a pound rather than to have to pay eighteen cents a pound for it? There is a wide constituency in this country who would rather pay five cents less for a dozen eggs than five cents more. There are an immense number of people scattered from Vancouver island to Cape Breton who would like, if they could have it, to have their bacon for fifteen cents a pound instead of paying nineteen cents a pound for it. My right hon. friend, in his cogitations in his bed at night and in his walks by day, says: There is the biggest constituency to be tapped in this country. You just go to them with the propaganda that, if they put you into power, you will give them their eggs for five cents less a dozen, their beef for five cents less a pound, and all their food products at a reduction; and if you do not capture all of them, because there are a good many sensible people in this country, you will stand to capture quite a number of the unthinking crowd. We will make that No. 1 of our new policy. Then he says:	There is the
farming class, a large class, the dominant class, the basic class in this country. Every farmer would rather have free agricultural implements than to have to pay even a small tax upon them. We may not get all the farmers toy making an appeal for free agricultural implements, but we may get a certain number of them and shall have a wide constituency to which to appeal, and a splendid electioneering ground. We will make that No. 2 of our new party policy. Again he looks upon the West and says: The Grain Growers' Company, the Agricultural Association, the man who follows the plough and who operates the reaper, all would like to get their agricultural implements cheaper by the amount of the duty, if it could be done. We shall have a large operating ground there if we adopt the plank of free agricultural implements. My right hon. friend, if I am not misrepresenting him, came to this House and met his party with the firm view that free food, free agricultural implements, and free wheat should be the slogan with which they would next appeal to the electorate. My right hon. friend has had to omit the largest and widest part of this propaganda; but am I wrong cr

right in saying that, what my right hon. friend has pitched upon, is not a policy which he has based upon the needs of the country and the best interest of the nation at large, but the particular policy upon which he thought, under all the circumstances, he could combine his following as an appeal for party advantage and for party plans, if possible. That, I think, is a fair version of this matter. I doubt if my right hon. friend will succeed; in fact, I have no faith that he will succeed. Why? Because it is not statesmanlike ground, because it is not national ground; it is an appeal to section and class, and no appeal to section and class will be ultimately successful in this country, and no appeal to section and class is a national appeal in this country or will square itself with the national feeling and aims of this country. My right hon. friend says:	If it is to be
a choice between two, I will take the farmer and give him his implements free rather than take the manufacturing industry concerned with the making of agricultural implements in this country, and give it even a small protection.
I will take my stand between those two. He says the same with reference' to the wheat growers and the wheat millers, and he thereby differentiates between classes in the basing of a national fiscal policy which, if it has any solid basis, must have one of principle and not of expediency. By what methods of reasoning can he justify the basing of an economic fiscal policy upon simply the demands of one or another class without taking into consideration the whole nation, the whole pact of industry, the whole pact of production? My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) uttered a truth in his free trade speech the other night when he said, 'You cannot favour one and discriminate against another in this matter of tariff policy.' So my hon. friend made himself an out-and-out free trader. There he is consistent, if he has the courage to carry it out in his political work. But it is dangerous ground and weak ground to go upon to pick out two or three .classes for special favours in tariff matters and base your fiscal policy for the whole country upon ground of that kind. Why? Because in the first place, it is neither fair nor just, and, in the second place, it does not tend to security. A fiscal platform should be based upon something which has principle, so that the great mass of the people may know upon what they can depend. What dependence is there if you base a tariff upon picking
out this and that and the other for special tariff favours? Every other industry, going along on a certain basis, does not know at what moment there may be another picking out, another alignment for the same purpose which will interfere with their business. With such an alignment as that you produce a feeling of insecurity and a lack of stability in your tariff which will react upon the stability and development of the industries of this country.
In regard to free wheat, my right hon. friend uttered what almost every speaker on that side of the House has uttered, a statement something like this: The farmer asks free wheat; why not give the farmer what he asks ? Will the members on both sides of the House just let that settle into their minds, and see where it leads us ? The appeal is made that in a matter of fiscal legislation we must base ourselves upon this as a proposition: If any one interest asks a certain thing, then they know more about that thing than anybody else does; give them what they ask. Is that possible as a basis for fiscal legislation ? Is it possible for Canada to proceed upon that basis ? I say it is not; I say that the tariff of this country is inter-related, every industry almost with every other, and the very moment you admit the principle that, if one particular industry must have what it wants in the way of fiscal legislation because it wants it and has most to do with it, you will be on a basis as unstable as water and as liable to injustice as anything possibly can be, which will work for the downfall of any fiscal system based upon it. Let us see how far that goes. The farmer wants free wheat in the West. Why ? Because it will be to his advantage in the way of price. His business will be better, he thinks, if he has free wheat. He therefore says: My interest lies in the direction of free wheat; give me that on the fiscal calendar and I will make more money. The miller comes in and says: I have to do with the grinding of wheat; I know this business and know it perfectly; my interest lies in giving me a certain fiscal line on my wheat. Why do you not listen to the miller as well as to the farmer ? If you are going to single out one class and take the dictum of that class and base your legislation upon it, to be consistent you will have to do it with other classes as well. I believe the farmers of this country know that of all classes they are most interested in having a populous, prosperous and progressive country in which to conduct their operations. There is no industry more

tied to its habitat than is the farmer's industry. The broker is here to-day and there to-morrow; the small manufacturer, while, to a certain extent tied to a locality, yet finds it comparatively easy to change. But the farming community is settled upon its acres, thousands of miles away from a distant market, and its prosperity depends upon filling up the country with a population that consumes the farm products, it depends upon the establishment and maintenance of a good home market. Calculate the value of the products of agriculture in this Dominion, and substract the comparatively small amount of the exports, and you find that probably eighty per cent of what the farmers of this country produce is consumed within the bounds of the Dominion. So, the farmer is vitally interested in having the industries of the country at their highest level of efficiency and their widest range of distribution. And I do not think the farmer himself is oblivious to this; I take it to be true that from 1878 up to the present time the mass of the farming population has been absolutely in accord with the general protective policy of this country because it has brought to them a great and prosperous home market. Nor is the farmer averse to paying his proportion of the taxes involved.
I remember, not so many years ago, when the duty on agricultural implements was thirty-five per cent. That was reduced to twenty per cent under the Liberal Conservative regime. There was a reduction under the Liberal Government of two and a half per cent, and a further reduction was made by my hon. friend (Mr. White) a few days ago of five per cent. So, in coming down from thirty-five per cent to twelve and a half per cent-all but two and a half per cent of which reduction has been made by the Liberal Conservative party-if agricultural implements are to-day at the call of the farmers of a country whose policy is a policy of protection at no more than twelve and a half per cent, I believe the farmers do not object to paying that duty as their contribution to the revenues. For the farmers, as a class, have had very much done for them. Every Government, whether that of my right hon. friend or that of the party opposed to him, has had a favoured and favouring face towards the farmers. In the way of experimental farms and stations, in the way of education, in the way of experiments in seeds and everything else, hundreds of thousands and millions of money have been expended for the benefit of the agricultural, stock raising and

dairying industries of this country. There is not one class that has had so much attention paid to them-and rightly so-as have the farmers of this country. And they quite understand that.
Now, I wish to say this in connection with free wheat: My right hon. friend thinks is i* an easy thing to single out wheat and put it on the free list and not run up against
difficulties. My mind does not run in that way. This question has its relation to a great many other industries. In the first place, let us follow the matter up to see who will get the benefit of the increase in price supposing there is such an increase. The argument of my right hon. friend is: Give free wheat so that the farmers of the West can get a number of cents per bushel more by having the United States market opened to him. But if you have a country that has a surplus of 140,000,000 or 150,000,000 bushels of wheat and you open up the market of a surplus country directly alongside of it having a surplus of 180,000,000 to
200,000,000, what happens in the rush for the fall market? What happened in the rush for the fall market when the United States market was not open but the Liverpool market, the distant market, was open? On account of the quick sale of the bulk of the crop in the Northwest the market price of the wheat went below the normal and stayed there. This occurred in the year when the best wheat that ever was raised, and the largest percentage of good wheat that ever was raised, was harvested in the northwest. But change your market to Minneapolis and St. Paul, where for three months wheat has been coming in in steady streams from the more southern parts of the United States, seek that market at a time when the Dakotas, north and south, and Wisconsin come in, and bring in your 150,000,000 or 200,000,000 bushels of wheat from Canada's Northwest and I ask you, will not that have the effect of reducing the price of wheat during the time of that rush? And it is during the time of that rush that the man who raises the grain is getting the grain out of his hands and delivering it over to the man who buys and speculates in grain. My opinion is that free wheat and the rush to the market from the Northwest into Minneapolis and St. Paul will depress the price of wheat during the time of the rush market and the farmer will get less for his wheat than he otherwise would. The man who will reap the benefit is the buyer, the storer, the speculator who buys it at its lowest, keeps it and sells it when it goes highest. So, you can-

not carry to every farmer of the West the pleasing thought that he is going to get an increased price for the wheat he has raised, because he cannot keep the wheat on his _ farm and regulate it to the uniform outflow that will give him any chance to keep the market from breaking. So, as I say, the boon will not be to the farmer who raises the wheat, but, if there is any advantage, it will go to the buyer, the speculator, the storer of wheat in the later of the many stages of the grain on its way to the final market.
But in considering the question of free wheat you have to have in mind other interests than those of the man who raises the wheat; you cannot give free wheat without disturbing other interests as well. You either believe or you do not believe that if free wheat were given, the bulk of the wheat in the West would go over to the American side; it would be of no benefit to open up the United States market unless it did go to the other side. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) is the greatest philosopher I have ever known. He first declared that if the wheat did not go to the United States, no harm would be done; he then declared that if it did go to the United States, no harm would be done, and he capped the whole thing by saying that it did not make any difference to him which way it went.
No, no.

Then I will leave out the
personal part of it and say that his assertion was that it did not particularly matter whether the wheat went one way or the other. I submit that that is not a statesmanlike characterization of the position. Is my hon. friend absolutely certain that the farmer who raises the grain will get the advantage of a single additional cent in the price of his product if free wheat is given?
. Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: I was arguing not about the price, ibut about a market for the increasing production; that is the most interesting side of the question.

I will come to that later. The question as to whether or not under free wheat the farmer who raises the wheat will get higher prices is an important one. Is my hon. friend certain that he will? To a large extent it is a matter of opinion, a matter of reasoning. Neither the hon. member for Halifax nor my right hon. friend is able to say that the farmer will
actually get a better price for his wheat. It is arguable on the other side that under the circumstances which I have mentioned he will get a lower price for his wheat.
My hon. friend will not deny that the British market will still be open to the Canadian wheat exporter if he does not get a better price.

If the wheat goes to the United States it is certain that a great many important interests in our country will be affected-interests for the protection and guidance of which we have spent immense sums of money. My right hon. friend, when he initiated his transcontinental railway policy, declared that that policy was justified, no matter what the expense, because what we wanted was to get an outlet for the products of the West. Later, in Montreal, he declared that he would never rest until every bushel of wheat raised in the West went out via the port of Montreal. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on great transport lines in the West in order to carry our wheat over our own lines to our own ports, en route to the European markets, in whatever part of the continent that may be. If free wheat results in the grain being carried from the West down to Minneapolis, St. Paul and Duluth, to that extent it takes away from the freightage upon our roads, upon which we have spent millions of money in order to carry out the products of our country. That is incidental, but such conditions would militate against the transportation interests of our country in so far as our great transcontinental lines are concerned. The adoption of free wheat would also run up against every other interest which is concerned in the handling and transporting of wheat-elevators, shipping marine, sea ports and Canadian ocean marine.
My right hon. friend does not feel absolutely certain, nor can he, that the Canadian miller, if free wheat is given and the wheat goes to the United States, will be able to carry on and extend his milling operations-for their extension is quite as important as their being successfully carried on. He is not able to say that the Canadian miller will be able to do this, but he thinks that he ought to. He believes that he will, but very careful thought must be given to the matter before you introduce such a change in your fiscal policy as will place so great an industry as the milling industry of this country in a position of peril.

A thought which has occurred to me just now is, I believe, one that is worthy of consideration. What is the whole trend of our commercial advancement and the upbuilding of our nationality? It is not the old-time idea of taking out the raw material which is of less value and disposing of it in a foreign market. The whole trend of our policy from 1878 up to the present time has been that we should throw all possible influences around what will conduce to the greatest amount of handling of the raw products that we raise in our own country. In so far as you encourage the idea that the raw wheat should be run off at a nearby market at an advantage on present prices, to that extent you strengthen the policy of taking one of the finest and most prolific of the products of this country out of Canada in its raw state and of taking with it the by-products which ought, to find their place in our own country. Is it not a fact that if the milling power of the great West could be used to the full extent of its present capacity, it would almost double the present market which is given to western wheat by the fnillers? If the milling industry is an industry which takes the raw product, divides it, separates it into portions and gives it for food and feed and for various otheT additions and helps to the other productions of the country, is it not the wisest thing for us to have all the wheat we can, milled in our own country and use and export the product rather than run it out of the country as raw material?
Would the hon. gentleman tell us where Canada would sell this additional product of the mill?

I will come to that later. So far as mixed farming in the old and in the new provinces is concerned, I do not know whether I am right or not, but I can see some features in the situation of the last two years in the western and eastern provinces which, to my mind, are due to certain causes. This depression has been less felt in the eastern than in the western provinces. Why? Because in the eastern provinces the home market has been more dense and more valuable; because in the eastern market there has been less speculation and consequently less waste and extravagance. You do not hear very much talk about depression from the farmers of the province of Ontario. Why? Because their products are varied; the salvation of the eastern provinces in these hard times has been in the varied nature of their products.
fMr. G. E. Foster.]
If there is not a high value for their barley, they use it in the production of stock and make up for it in that way.
They have various products which they can sell in the home market; and it is that variety of production and the greater density of the home market, with the comparative absence of speculation, that differentiates the situation in the East from the situation in the West. How are you going to get back to a proper readjustment in the West? You will get back to it in proportion as you introduce and strengthen those conditions; and not by legislation to any very great extent, hut by a reformation and a readjustment amongst the people themselves, you will cure the causes that have led to the present condition of things. Now, Sir, if it be true that the salvation of the West must be dependent on its going more and more into mixed farming, if you obliterate milling or weaken the milling industry of the Northwest, how do you act upon the greatest factor of mixed farming in the Northwest, and the feed that is absolutely necessary for raising the varied animal products that you should have in the West? So it seems to me that a policy which would militate in favour of drawing the raw material out of the country rather than manufacturing it to the greatest possible extent in the country itself, would not be in the best interests of the Northwest itself.

If the United
States put wheat on the free list themselves we would be in -the same danger then?

Exactly, and if a man burns down my house I am not fool enough to say I wish I had burned that down myself so that he could not do it. I look to our great West, we all look to it, to be the great centre of our country for many, many years to come. Everything which [DOT] tends to make easier the growth and export of grain for itself, as an exclusive industry, on the farm lands of the West, tends to impoverish and rob the virtue from the soil which is to compete in after years and after ages with the countries of the world in the products which come from that soil. Therefore I think that it looks very much like a nature cure which has taken place. There has been a rush to the sole raising of wheat. There is now a marked diversion towards mixed farming. The circumstances of the last year and of to-day will give an impetus to the mixed farming development of the West by the

very fact that the price of grain is approaching a point where it will be more profitable for a man in the West to put at least a certain amount of his grain growing capacity into mixed farming, to feed stock and raise dairy produce.
Would the minister tell us what we will do with the stock? Will we export it or will we put on an export duty? Our beef is exported now, as the minister knows.

I would not like to credit my hon. friend with not knowing what to do with his stock when he got it ready for market. I think he would dispose of it very quickly. It is far better, that instead, for instance, of selling off his sucking pigs and his young calves that he should put them into the shape of the weightiest pork and the best beef and the best stockers before he sells them. That is all I am asking and that, I think, is good policy for this country. My hon. friend calls to my mind one of his arguments. He was arguing the other day that 25,000,000 bushels of oats went out of this country since the Underwood tariff came in force and he said that every bushel of oats had to pay six cents customs duty and that therefore on that 25,000,000 bushels just $1,500,000 less was received by the producer of the oats than if that duty of six cents had not been on. That is an easy calculation, easily done with pencil and paper, but does my hon. friend's practical sense follow that argument upon paper? If so I will put another phase of it to him. The former duty on oats, the season before last was fifteen cents per bushel. This year it is but six cents. Therefore the seller of that
25,000,000 bushels of oats by the reasoning of my hon. friend is just $2,500,000 better ofi than he would have been last year. The same kind of reasoning applies to everything that has been put on the free list or on the reduced list by the Underwood tari0. If you take wheat on which the duty is now only ten cents against twenty-five cents, if you take cattle, beef, everything, sum it up and you can just add to it the number of cents per pound or per bushel of duty that has been taken ofi by the Underwood tariff, and according to the hon. member, a perfect flood of money has rushed into that great Northwest and is now in the hands of the farmers. But my hon. friend says that you did not do that, that was 181
done by the Underwood tariff. I am not denying it, but is it therefore of any less advantage to the farmer o.f the West and how is it that to-day the farmers in the West are poorer than they were last year and have less money to send down to the East for manufactured products when the
25,000,000 bushels of oats put $2,500,000 cash into the hands of the sellers and they also received innumerable millions on the stock and other products that have gone to the United States under the Underwood tariff? I do not like to say that I do not subscribe altogether to the remarks of my hon. friend from Humboldt, but ,1 am bound to say to him that if his argument is right there are a great many things to be accounted for that he has not accounted for in his philosophy. My hon. friend from Halifax has asked: where will we get a market for our wheat.
Oh no, I did not; the hon. gentleman was arguing that all the wheat which we grew should be ground into flour and I asked him to tell me where we would find a market for that flour.
I have not argued that all our grain must be ground into flour.
You have made an elaborate argument.

I am arguing for a policy which will give an impulse in the direction of grinding in our country as much of our wheat into flour as possibly can be ground. I make the same argument with reference to every other natural product of our country. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) asked as to where we could get a market for our wheat and for our flour. He declared that Great Britain consumed a certain amount, of which we supplied a fractional part at the present time, and he did not think there was any chance for an expansion of the market in Great Britain, particularly for flour. Afterwards, when he was trying to meet the argument that if the wheat went across the border there would be nothing left for our own railways to transport, he declared that he expected to see in the near future the products of grain in different kinds going out in ever-increasing quantities over our own transport system via the Hudson bay and the St. Lawrence, and through St. John and Halifax. I can pose the same question to him that he posed to the House in the early part of his speech: 'Where do



you expect to get a market? Now, the question of markets troubles people to a certain extent, and yet there is a vast undeveloped market that this country has at hand. Let me for a moment refer to a table that I have prepared. It shows the value of wheat imported into the great wheat-consuming countries-not producing countries-and the total volume of flour imported into flour-consuming countries. It totals up to this: These great market countries-deficit markets, so to call them-imported wheat last year to the value of $844,-
954,000,	and of that amount Canada sent only $65,000,000 worth to fill that vast demand. Flour was imported into flour-consuming countries to the value of $82,171,000, and of that Canada sent only $16,161,000 worth. Taking wheat and flour together, there was a market of $727,000,000, of which Canada supplied $81,000,000 worth. There is, then, a vast market to which Canada can appeal with her good wheat and her good flour in competition with the world, and it is in competition with the world that she will have to sell her wheat and her flour whether at Minneapolis, Rotterdam, or Liverpool. There is also a vast unfilled market for farmers' products in this country, and for the products of our different industries as well. I think that the difficulty to-day is not to find markets for what Canada produces; and not that we do not get into the United States market, but is to be found in other directions. One thing is, I think, certain, and with that I propose to close my remarks: taking it by and large, the country which has a surplus of any product must seek its market in that country which has not a surplus of that product; and taking it by and large, it is not defensible that a country which has a surplus of 200,000,000 bushels of wheat should seek its natural or profitable market in a country that has a surplus of about the same quantity. It strikes me that it is something like this: Two farmers are travelling along the great road, each with an immense wagon load of wheat. One is Johnny Canuck and the other is Uncle Sam. Uncle Sam says: I have a large family of nearly one hundred millions of people; I have supplied them for the year with all the wheat and flour that they need, and now I am carrying on my truck to sell in the European market about two hundred million bushels of surplus for which there is no market in my own country. Johnny Canuck says:	I have a family o; about
eight millions of people, and I have sup-
plied them with all the wheat and flour they need for this year. I have a surplus of about 150,000,000 bushels which I have in my cart here and I am headed for the very same market that you are heading for, Uncle Sam, to sell my surplus product. Johnny Canuck thinks a moment and says: Why not you take this, Uncle Sam, then I can turn my steps and go home; buy my wheat from me? But Uncle Sam says:	I
have more than I want, and am looking for a purchaser myself. And so they haggle till a bright idea strikes Uncle Sam and he says:	Very well, Johnny, I will take
your wheat. I have quite a large family, and I will set some of them carrying your wheat down to the seaports; others shall mill some of it in their mills; I will set hundreds of thousands of people to work on that wheat of yours, all getting some profit out of it and adding to its value until at last it is sent to Liverpool and London, its ultimate market. But, Johnny, I cannot do that unless I get your grain at a price which will enable me to do it at profit to myself. That is, Uncle Sam will be the broker, the handler, the manager and the profit maker; he will act in that friendly way for Canada. But why should we not do that work ourselves? Then Uncle Sam says: In the back of my head I have another idea. We are great raisers of cattle, hogs, and sheep in my country. If I take your wheat I will manipulate it on its way to London so that it will make millions of pounds of the best feeding material for my stock, as well; and, Johnny, after I have done all that, and fattened my cattle and hogs for market whatever surplus I have will meet you in London and Liverpool when you go over there to sell your surplus products.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. MICHAEL CLARK (Red Deer). Mr. Speaker, the significant absence of any Government member at nearly five minutes past eight would almost seem to indicate that after the speech of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) the Government was seriously contemplating resigning. Even now the only ministers to turn up are my good, genial friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White), who is very attentive to his post, and my equally good friend (Mr. Rogers), who is very likely to leave us for a higher position across the Atlantic. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has been living a good

deal of the last two and a half years at sea-
Oh, oh.

I mean actually at sea.
This afternoon he was still at sea metaphorically. I do not think that even the warmest of the hon. gentleman's admirers will consider that that very able gentleman did anything this afternoon to add to his great reputation as a debater and somewhat of an economist. His speech consisted in a few quips at my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in which he is a past master, in his getting hopelessly fogged in figures concerning flour, and in the very moderate rehash of an argument extending to an hour and a half, an argument which took four hours previous to the reciprocity agreement of two and a half years ago, or the attempted reciprocity agreement. The minister himself said that there were two courses open to him; one was to discuss the speaker who had preceded him, and the other was to dwell upon the general financial situation and the general field of thought and discussion presented in the Budget. He chose the one of confining himself to a reply to my right hon. friend who preceded him. I shall, for one particular reason at any rate, take the opposite course. I propose to devote myself to what I think the people of the country are vastly more interested in than a duel between such veterans as crossed swords this afternoon. I shall devote myself to that which I believe the country is very much interested in and that is the general financial situation and the way that financial situation is dealt with in the Budget speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. I ought also to say that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce very courteously told me that he had a previous engagement at St. George's Society, and could not be here this evening. I shall all the more gladly only refer to his speech as it is necessary to do so in the general course of my remarks.
I want to follow the example which has been very general and congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Finance upon the qualities which appear to me to have characterized the Budget speech which he delivered. It was a matter of very great regret that I could not listen to his speech; circumstances beyond my control took me into the West, but I read it with the utmost care and it appeared to be characterized by 181i
very great lucidity, very great candour, considerable inconsistency, and not more than the average of the fallacies that are sure to overtake any one who attempts to defend protection. There was another quality in the speech which was commented upon by my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). I take it that he formed his judgment as to that quality being present partly from the matter of the speech and partly from the manner of it. As I did not hear the speech I only got the impression from the matter. The quality to which I refer was the very great change from the previous speeches of the Minister of Finance in this House. The previous year when he was handling the condition of the country, as it was immediately bequeathed to him, good times, accompanied by surpluses and trade expansion, he spoke in tones which reached what I might venture to call a key of shrill falsetto. He was very well satisfied with the result of the last elections and with the condition of the country and that was the tone se spoke in. This year he was dealing with his own production and he struck a distinctly minor key better suited to the times.
I am glad the minister admitted, however, that we are having times of depression. I noticed that the admission has not been quite general on the other side of the House. No one has denied it but there has been a tendency on the part of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to seek for a depression in the ranks of theiT opponents. They have referred to our speeches as indicating some sort of pessimism on this side of the House. I do not know what is the actual state of mind of those by whom I am surrounded but I think it is not different from my own and I will say there is no pessimism on this side of the House which is in the slightest degree discreditable to us whether as good party men or good Canadians. There is no one on the other side of the House who has any more profound belief than I have in the greatness of the destiny of this country. There is no one on the other side of the House who is surer that his party is sailing in good water in this Budget debate than I am. Hon. gentlemen mistake us. We are not pessimistic about Canada. Our pessimism is about the present Government. I think that before I finish I shall be able to reveal the grounds of the pessimism and show that it is well founded.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce had a somewhat light and easy way of dealing with the depression of the country. He said

this thing is just like a man taking a sleep and he will wake up again all light-meaning Canada. If he had said that the Government was asleep I should have been in agreement with him. It is not Canada that is asleep. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is rather drowsy and he has not got over the tropical seas and climes through which he has been sailing and the whole Government is asleep. Our pessimism is not on the ground of Canada but on the ground of the Government. The Minister of Finance, conscious of his position, differing as it does from that of former years, perfectly conscious and perfectly candid about it, takes refuge in the proposed universality of the depression. He says it is a cycle of bad trade and that we are in the cycle. I do not admit his contention. I do not think he can establish it. I shall take it as regards the United States. Even in the short time that the Wilson-Underwood tariff has been in operation it has produced a marvellous effect upon the condition of commerce in the United States, and has given an enormous impetus to the trade of that country. The other day 2,000,000 pounds of wool arrived in Boston harbour from our colony of Australia, a record for the port. What is happening to that wool? It is going into the factories of the United States; and I read in the Daily Chronicle of London that, as a result of that and other like imports, nearly all the factories of the United States are working overtime. The very moderate reduction of the tariff which has taken place in that country has given an enormous impetus to commerce there. At the very time when our trade is shrinking, if we judge by our trade returns, the trade of the United States is expanding. I do not admit, as regards our neighbouring country, the universality which the minister claims for this condition of depression, much less do I admit it with regard to the United Kingdom. In Great Britain it is notorious that for the last three years they have been passing through times of phenomenal prosperity. The pauperism last January was the lowest in Great Britain that has ever been recorded either in the aggregate of paupers or in the pauperism per thousand. These are facts and one could multiply them indefinitely to show that this condition that the minister admits is not world-wide, and does not apply to the two countries with which we in Canada are most intimately connected, which we most intimately resemble and towards the condition of which whether as to adversity or as to prosperity, we will 
most nearly approximate. I want to urge that our Government are in a very large measure responsible for the existing condition. They are face to face with that responsibility and they will have to face it before the people of this country.
In a recent debate my right hon. friend the Prime Minister referred to the legacy in regard to railroads that had come down from the previous Administration. He charged upon the previous Government the difficulties in regard to railroads with which this Administration is saddled. It is not a very noble method, when a man gets into a scrape, to blame the otheT fellow; but, if it is not very noble, it is very ancient; it originated in the garden of Eden, so that it is very human as well as very ancient. I do not want to minimize any force there is in that argument or in any fair argument of an opponent. I think I used sentences myself, during the course of this session, which would indicate that we had a considerable load of railroads for the size of this country and for the number of people in the country. But I think it is a fair reply to that argument of my right hon. friend; it is a fair rejoinder in the face of that argument to say that, if there was some legacy of railroads which was not as good as it might have been, that legacy was accompanied by a condition of tremendous prosperity in the country and by a surplus of some $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 in the treasury. There is nothing in the railroads of Canada to frighten the people of Canada, if the policy of the Government of Canada is right. Take the condition of that western country and our railroads. As my Tight hon. friend the leader of the Opposition pointed out in his speech this afternoon, we have tilled some six per cent of the possible arable land of Canada, and the Canadian Pacific railway has built up upon that fractional tillage a prosperity and a greatness almost beyond the dreams of human avarice. If the policy of the Government is wisely directed to an increase of the production of the wealth which is possible in western Canada, is there any Canadian so poor spirited that he sees any difficulty in making the other two railroads of Canada as prosperous? This is not the only thing that the previous Government bequeathed; they bequeathed to the country these railroads; they bequeathed to the country the prosperity and the enormous surplus to which I have referred. If they had not been defeated by the party opposite and by argu-

ments, which even Ontario will one day regret, which she is regretting now, we would have carried out a policy in this country which would have gone to maintain fully the prosperity which characterized the fifteen years, of Liberal rule. I charge it upon this Government that the defeat of reciprocity is largely responsible for the condition in which the country is found to-day. Just as the lowering of the tariff against Great Britain was followed by an enormous increase of our international commerce, by great land settlement, by increase of our wealth and of our prosperity, so a farther widening of our markets would have brought about a similar result.
I want to say farther that the hard times, which have been prevented by the extension of our markets, have been tremendously aggravated by the extravagance of the present Government. In my judgment, the expenditure of this country in the two and one-half years that this Government has been in power has gone up in a way that is reprehensible, indefensible and unnecessary. It has gone up in that way against the most specific and fair warnings that ever were addressed by an opponent to a gentleman in the position of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. My hon. friend, the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), in his first Budget criticism, warned my hon. friend of his duty in this matter. The Minister of Finance was new to political life, he was new to the duties of his office and the junior member for Halifax warned him thit he was surrounded by colleagues who wouid characterize his Government as an extravagant Government, and in spite of that;, the . Minister of Finance neglected his first duty [DOT]and invited extravagance. His very first duty towards the people of this country was to keep a tight watch upon the treasury. He is the custodian of the national moneys. There are what are called the spending departments of the Government, but it is my hon. friend's duty in his office to be the watch dog of the treasury and to hold those spending departments off except for what is absolutely necessary. That is a very serious charge to bring against my hon. friend. I have charged him with inviting extravagance, or, if I have not, I charge him with it now, and I am going to prove it in his own words. I listened with great interest, as I always do when he speaks, to his Budget speech of last session, at the close of which he used these words:
I do not believe-
This was in spite of the warnings of my hon. friend.
-in a Government curtailing expenditure simply because it appears that on account of financial depression there might be a limitation of trade.
There is a specific declaration of policy on the part of my hon. friend. What does it immediately commit him to? If trade is limited-and twelve months ago he seemed to foresee a limitation of our trade -it meant a limitation of revenue, for our revenue is collected under a tariff, and its extent depends on the foreign trade of the country. Limitation of trade meant diminished revenue, and there has been only one course open to the minister, and that was to borrow money, and he has indicated in this Budget his intention to-continue that policy. I think myself that is most unsound finance, and I should be wanting in my duty both to my hon. friend and to the country if I did not state that opinion and the grounds upon which I base it.
I think it is most unsound finance to extend our borrowings in a condition such as that of Canada at the present moment. And that opinion seems to be .shared by those who lend money in the old country; because from the hon. gentleman's experience in that country I rather think they did not quite smile upon his most recent efforts in the direction of borrowing. My hon. friend justifies borrowing by a very old argument. He says we are using the money that we borrow to effect improvements, part of the benefit of which posterity will get, and therefore it is right that we should leave posterity to pay part of the cost. Well, the investors in the old country did not seem to have the .unlimited belief in my hon. friend's posterity that he himself has. Nor do I think there is any soundness in -his argument. I have never read of a posterity in the past that did not have enough trouble with its own finances, its own expenditures and its own times. I may not have as strong an imagination as the hon. minister's, but certainly I cannot imagine a posterity in a world constituted as this is that will not have trouble enough of its own. I think this is unsound finance and based on unsound reasoning. In this speech the hon. gentleman went farther and said:
We have a population to-day of eight millions, and it will soon be ten millions, fifteen mi' * lions, twenty-five millions.
Let me say to my hon. friend that the realm of figures is a very, very bad realm indeed, in which to introduce too much imagination. When the Minister of

Finance, introducing too much imagination into the realm of figures, thinks of this country as having a population of twenty-five millions, in an administration like his he can always find a Minister of Militia who will immediately begin to spend upon the twenty-five million basis. And that is exactly what happened to my hon. friend. He stood at the treasury box of the country, of which he ought to be the guardian and watchdog, and he practically said: ' Come along; dip in.' And the Minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes) dipped in. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) rejoices in his ability to spend money and in his department, as a spending department. I would like my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to consult the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster). In spite of the speech he made this afternoon, there are some good things about the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I am sure if the Minister of Finance were to consult him about some of the things I am saying he would say I was preaching sound doctrine. I know he would, for when he went to South Lanark recently, he told the people that the cure for bad times was to be frugal, careful, and economical. I have no objection to the Minister of Trade and Commerce delivering advice like that in South Lanark; but he should know that advice, like charity, should begin at home, and I wish he would give that advice to the Finance Minister.
I wish to impress upon the Finance Minister that the farther he goes on this course the more he will find out that a nation, no more than a man, can spend and borrow and tax itself into prosperity. It has never been done in the world. I have referred before to my hon. friend's illustration of the Prodigal Son; and he knows that the Prodigal Son was not a success along that line. He spent himself into adversity, and I have known many people do the same. But no man or government can spend themselves into prosperity; it is contrary to reason and common sense. Borrowing as a policy, cannot be too strongly condemned, especially in a country like ours, in the case of a federal government. For the federal government is imitated by the provincial governments, and these by the municipalities, and the result is that we get into the position in which we are in Canada today a position of hard times in a country inhabited by a people who are capable of the greatest things but have the handicap at the present time of being the most indebted people in the world per capita, taking all their debts, municipal, provincial
{Mr. M. Clark.]
and federal. I think that statement is capable of proof past all possible doubt.
I would like to follow this a little farther in order to impress it upon the minis-' ter. I know that we never talk economy in this country; the extravagance of the present day, I have no doubt, will make my words sound very old-fashioned. But it does not trouble me to hold and to proclaim an unpopular opinion. I had the pleasure to follow the greatest man I am likely to look upon in this world when, twenty-eight years ago, he went down to defeat in an effort to give Home Rule to Ireland. It has taken twenty-eight years to give Home Rule to Ireland, but I do not think that even Sir Edward Carson will be able to prevent it much longer. It may take me even longer to succeed with free trade, but I know it will not take me nearly so long to succeed with my teachings with regard to economy, for when a man or Government spends too much, Providence steps in and sees to it that they do not get what they want to spend, and though they may run through one fortune, they do not readily get another. I desire to cite an article in the Statist of February last, which, I think, any one can read with great profit and which will explain exactly what we borrowed last year, what happened to our borrowings, and what the effect was upon the commerce of the world and upon Canada as a nation. In the debate on the address I referred to the fact-and the minister was good enough to agree with me-that when we borrow we do not borrow money but credit, and everything we borrow comes into the country in the shape of commodities. Now what actually happened with regard to the borrowings of Canada in 1913, according to this article in the Statist? We borrowed credit and immediately transferred that credit in London to the United States by buying goods from the United States with that credit. The United States did not immediately buy from Great Britain, but with the credit which we had transferred to them, the United States proceeded to buy coffee, rubber and other produce from Brazil, importing last year three times as much from Brazil as they sold to that country; they proceeded to buy tea, jute and other products from India, importing four times as much from India as they exported to India; they proceeded to buy silk and other produce from Japan, their imports from Japan being very much in excess of their exports to Japan.

I sum often called a theorist, tout this is not theorizing; these are the actual facts concerning the trade of these countries during the last year. Our original credit borrowed in London and transferred in this way was finally discharged by these three nations, Brazil, Japan and India, taking last year unprecedented quantities of wool, cotton and machinery from the old country -and so the circuit was made. I want the minister to think of that for a moment.
I have no reason to assume that he is not cognizant of the facts, but I want this House to think of them for a moment. What has happened ? Our borrowings last year-this ought to be extremely interesting to those who preach a national policy for the building of home industry-our borrowings last year promoted to an enormous extent the industries of the United States, to an enormous extent the industries of . Britain, to an enormous extent the industries of Japan, of Brazil and of India, and Canada was left with a debt and has the ' interest to pay on it. That is all that came to Canada for these borrowings last year; no promotion of the industry of Canada was made in the exchanges as between these countries. I think that these simple economic truths-and they are truths- ought to produce something to recommend to the minister my opinion that borrowing is an unsound line of policy.
I have been looking up some of the masters for the benefit of my hon. friend, if he would care to hear about them. I have been looking up some of the things that Mr. Gladstone said in a speech which I very well remember being delivered in Edinburgh in the year 1879, in which he laid down certain principles of finance. In that speech dealing with finance, and laying down these principles, he made the claim that the principles he was laying down were those that had built up the financial greatness of England in the beginning of its career; that they were the principles laid down alike by the Liberal and the Tory parties, and he claimed to have learned them from Sir Robert Peel. In laying down these principles he referred to Sir Robert Peel coming into power, not at a time of prosperity, as my hon. friend did, but in 1842, when Britain was in a state of adversity for which I think Canada has no parallel in her history. That was four years before protection was done away with in Britain. When Sir Robert Peel came into power in 1842, he found a deficit. I remember as if it were yesterday Mr. Gladstone on one occasion standing at his place at the table of the
House and saying: Shall I meet this condition by the miserable expedient of making provision by loans from year to year? Founding himself upon the high authority of Sir Robert Peel, Mr. Gladstone laid down the principle that each year should as far as possible provide by taxation for the expenditure of that year. That was one of his principles of finance. He went on further to say that he himself believed- and this was another principle of finance- that the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Minister of Finance, ought to aim at a surplus, for this specific reason: not only that it was necessary to avoid borrowing, but that an honest financier should always be endeavouring to wipe out the national debt. Mr. Gladstone laid it down a3 a sound principle of finance that a surplus should be aimed at as the main instrument for the steady reduction of the public debt of the country.
My hon. friend in answering the charges of extravagance which were brought against him last year in the Budget debate by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) said: the charge is too general; why do you not particularize? I think we have come to a time when particulars are being given to the minister. My hon. friend the* hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) did something in this line yesterday and I think I can particularize from an authority to whom even the Finance Minister would give considerable attention; I mean his chief in the Cabinet. I do not know how far it is within the recollection of hon. gentlemen that the right hon. leader of this Government said in the debate upon the naval resolution of five years ago that in his opinion at least half of the money spent upon the militia at that time might be diverted to the naval defence of the empire. If my hon. friend wants particulars he can take half the military expenditure of that time and put on several millions that have been spent since his Government came into power and he will get a good round sum in the way of detail with which to begin to practise economy in the handling of the moneys of the people of this country. He could, again, go to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and "Commerce for advice on this subject. A short time ago the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said that a great deal of money was being wasted on commissions in this county-commissions which were wasting a

good deal of ink and paper in the printing of reports which were laid upon shelves and never read. It is too late to save the $60,000 to $100,000 that has been spent on probably the most useless commission that ever sat in this country, the National Transcontinental Commission; but these are some of the particulars that I would like to call to the attention of the minister. Let me point out that it is not part of our duty to supply the minister with these particulars; he is the watchdog of the treasury and ought to find them out for himself. He knows what is going on within the Government; it is his duty to know these particulars. I want on that point to . finish my quotation from Mr. Gladstone's principles of finance by quoting to the minister-I am afraid it will fall on deaf ears in this country, almost in the case of any government, but I will quote nevertheless -the words in which Mr. Gladstone laid down what he called the first principle of finance:
The first of them is, that the Chancellor of the Exchequer shall boldly uphold economy in detail; and it is the mark, gentlemen, of, I was going to say a chicken-hearted Chancellor of the Exchequer when he shrinks from upholding economy in detail. He is ridiculed no doubt, for what is called saving candle-ends or cheeseparings. No chancellor of the exchequer is worth his salt who is not ready to save what are meant by candle-ends and cheese-parings in the cause of his country. No chancellor of the exchequer is worth his salt who makes his own popularity either his first consideration or any consideration at all, in administering the public purse.
My hon. friend is so agreeable a gentleman and I am so fond of him that I hate to say what I am going to say now, but unless he improves his ways we will have to say one of these days that as the guardian of the public treasury he is not worth his salt and to say that will hurt me more than it will hurt him.
This has been a rather dry lecture, I am afraid, but sometimes it is necessary to give dry lectures; at any rate the minister will not charge me with bringing too much imagination into the realms of finance.
When we turn to the trade of the country I think there is ground for anxiety. I want to say that the last thing I think any patriotic man should do is to exaggerate any financial depression we have, and I do not think that that is the duty of an opposition. But equally it is wrong to hide evident truths from the public view and especially from the view of those who are responsible for the Government of this

country. Taking the twelve months, the minister is just able to show an increase of our trade, but if he had taken the last six months he would have had a report that the trade of the country is declining. That is the fact as to the external trade of Canada at the present moment; there is not the expansion and the buoyancy that there has been in our trade for sixteen or seventeen years past. I very mudh doubt if the conditions of our trade are such as to give the optimistic outlook which the minister endeavours to maintain. Our imports have declined; that, from my point of view, is not wholly bad; it is not bad so far as it indicates a decline in our borrowings. In so far as it indicates fewer people coming into our country, I think, it is bad. I notice that my hon friend the Minister of the Interior, speaking in Montreal the other day, admitted that during this year we may look for a falling off of fifty per cent in our immigrants. It is the same in regard to immigrants as it is in regard to building of railroads, if we do not know what to do with immigrants when they come I agree with the minister that they should not be brought; but it is a melancholy confession that in a country with two people to a square mile you cannot so frame a policy that these people can make a living on the finest area of land ever cultivated in this or any other country. Our exports during recent months have been declining, and this is wholly bad because it means production has been reduced to a minimum, and the country is living from hand to mouth.
There is another aspect of the trade of the country of which I thought the minister would have had more to say because trade matters have been very much in dispute in this country in recent years and we have arrived at a point when, having regard to matters which were forward in the last election and which have been occupying the minds of the people and of Parliament ever since, we as an Opposition have a right to ask: How are the alternatives of the Government coming along in the way of providing for an external trade for this country?
I think we have a Tight to ask that and in asking it I am founding myself upon the example of my hon. friends when they were in opposition. I looked up the other day a book adorned with the features of the present Prime Minister and called ' Facts for the People/ and I read in that this statement of fact for the people: The Laurier Government has not opened to Canada a single foreign market. Now, that is a shady kind

of a fact to begin with, because the moment the Laurier Government came into power they introduced the British preference which gave us a market, resisted by our friends at the time but lauded high now. Immediately, as the result of .the British preference we got a tremendous hold on the British market in which we have been doing an ever-increasing business. But in addition to that the Government went out of power, as we have shown again and again, endeavouring to provide another market and it does not lie in the mouths of these gentlemen to say that the Laurier Government has not provided us with a single market. But what have they done in regard to markets? Well, of course, we heard a great deal this afternoon about the home market as we have been hearing throughout the whole of this debate. Anybody would think that the party opposite created the home market. Every country has its home market for the staple lines of its produce. In every country, in spite of the Government, whether the Government be Tory or Liberal, as soon as people begin to trade they trade in the home market. It is the only market they have. I wish my friends opposite would study the history of trade in this connection. An interesting theory was propounded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. A. Thompson) yesterday. My hon. friend is coming along very nicely in his economic studies. He was one of a number of members who made special reference to myself and he formulated a theory of trade that I could not quite endorse, but which went a considerable distance in the direction of the truth. He said: It appears that every country is free trade to begin with and then becomes protectionist and then gets back to free trade again. I think if we should go back right to the origin of trade we would find that to begin with every country is more or less protectionist; they are at any rate in regard to the home market. When there was nobody but the Indian in this country and he went out each morning and caught a little fish or killed a little venison and came home to the tepee and shared it with the squaw and the papooses, you had the ideal of protection theory realized, you had the home market for home consumption-you had Canada for the Canadians. So I think my hon. friend in his evolutionary theory did not go quite far enough back. In regard to free trade there is no doubt that his theory is quite correct. I am very anxious to believe it, and it was consolatory to myself to know it was coming. I
regret that he should think Canada is only qualified as yet to be in the backwoods stage of her development and 1 am sure that he and those by whom he is surrounded will never be angry with me because I want to hurry up their evolution.
Do our friends really believe all they have been saying about the home market? Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself believe that the home market is of the tremendous importance that he seemed to indicate this afternoon? He recommends as a cure for western conditions the building up of a home market in western Canada. That was the first portion of the cure that this Government proposed for present conditions, that is their first alternative. They are continually mentioning the policy on which we went down to defeat two and one-half years ago. I wish my friends would reflect that there never was a people who had to be so patient with advice as the representatives of the West and those whom they represent have had to be during this Budget debate. There is apparently not a man in Ontario who could not run the affairs of the West with the utmost ease if we would only put those affairs right into his individual hands. If we were dependent upon the home market in western Canada, as these gentlemen advise, I want to ask the Government what would happen to their elevator policy. Mixed farming is the cure, the home market is the cure for the West. In other words, we are only to grow enough wheat for western consumption. Then I charge it upon this Government that they are the most foolish people on the face of this earth, because they are spending an enormous amount of money on elevators and they are threatening to spend $150,000,000 on the Hudson Bay railroad, all of which is based upon the presumption that Canada is going to have an enormous outside trade in wheat. So that one part of these gentlemens' argument is thoroughly destructive of the other part. I want to bring to the attention of our hon. friends who talk about the home market in the West as a cure for our conditions. The elevators and the railways under those circumstances can only become monuments of the folly of the present Government. I want to tell our hon. friends something about the home market as it exists in the West to-day. Day before yesterday, in the last Albertan that came to hand from Calgary, I notice a statement that 4,000 hogs had been shipped from Calgary to the Seattle market in one day. That has been going on ever since the Wi'lson-Underwood tariff came into operation. If that tariff had not given us a relief for those
